prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: 街道便民服务中心一窗受理事项办理台账 (language zh-CN).
Grid: 3 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "序号" · longest unbreakable word 16px · one-line width 31px
  col 2: header "状态" · longest unbreakable word 16px · one-line width 46px
  col 3: header "内容" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 1932px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"序号 and 状态 are given huge ~210px columns holding one digit or three characters, so two-thirds of the table is empty white, while 内容 is squeezed into a narrow strip that wraps every row to 10–12 lines and makes the table very tall; scanning status across rows is easy but reading the substance is laborious."},"B":{"grade":"poor","why":"The content column gets generous width, but 序号 and 状态 are crushed: the header 序号 stacks vertically as 序/号 and status cells break into 已/办/结, destroying two short, comparison-critical fields and making the header row read as a vertical smear rather than a label."},"C":{"grade":"excellent","why":"序号 and 状态 are sized to their content (headers and 已办结/办理中/已退回 stay on one line) and all remaining width goes to 内容, giving ~4 balanced lines per row; the table is compact, the header hierarchy is clear and rows read as single units."},"D":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Essentially the same sensible proportion as C: minimal identifier and status columns, maximal content column, all short fields intact on one line, rows of even height and a clean rhythm down the page; nothing is wasted and nothing is cramped."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"Same good allocation, but the content column is a touch narrower than C/D, so a couple of rows gain an extra line and break mid-phrase; still readable and well balanced, just slightly less efficient."},"F":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The short columns are fine, but 内容 is noticeably narrower than in C/D/E, pushing most rows to five lines with more awkward breaks (e.g. dates and phrases splitting across lines) and a taller, more ragged table."}},"best":["D","C"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"C, D and E differ by only a few pixels, so their relative order is close to arbitrary; I inferred widths from the rendered separators rather than exact measurements."}
